text:
GRU4Rec’s official implementation recommends cross-entropy or BPR-max; ordinary BPR suffers vanishing gradients as negative sets grow. BPR-max emphasizes high-scoring negatives, but that does not identify whether they are truly irrelevant. Cross-entropy’s logQ sampling correction addresses sampling distribution bias, a different issue from false-negative contamination. These are useful controls before introducing semantic mining. [GRU4Rec implementation](https://github.com/hidasib/GRU4Rec)

Two relevant 2024 approaches: [Hard-BPR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19276) modifies the ranking objective specifically to reduce false-negative influence under dynamic hard sampling; [AHNS](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28709) adapts negative hardness during training instead of maintaining a fixed difficulty. Both report collaborative-filtering results, so transfer to this GRU4Rec benchmark remains unproven. A [2024 sequential-recommendation study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) finds sampling effects depend on dataset popularity structure, with aggregate metrics hiding head/mid/tail differences. The [2025 context-aware sampling paper](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/11021640) primarily improves diversity, reporting a small accuracy loss; it does not establish an HR@10 benefit here.

Practical hypothesis: separately compare BPR-max, sampling-corrected cross-entropy, and Hard-BPR or adaptive moderate-hard sampling using the same single GRU4Rec architecture and training-only histories. Exclude known training positives; retain some random negatives and vary hardness cautiously. These are proposed ablations, not established improvements. Keep text-based filtering separate: semantic similarity can indicate either useful competitors or unobserved positives. Electronics’ supplied 4.56% wrong-order rate measures discrimination against its sampled negatives; it cannot establish why validation ranking fails. Select by the pinned four-category macro validation HR@10.
